canberra.title: Boeing’s win in US Navy F/A-XX fighter competition gives it a next generation monopoly
canberra.snippet: The US Navy has announced that Boeing will build its next generation of combat aircraft. Currently dubbed F/A-XX, the new aircraft will r...
canberra.content:
F/A-XX concept art. Image: Boeing.

The US Navy has announced that Boeing will build its next generation of combat aircraft.

Currently dubbed F/A-XX, the new aircraft will replace the current Boeing F/A-18E/F fighters and EA-18G electronic attack aircraft onboard US Navy aircraft carriers from mid next decade.

The selection of Boeing effectively gives it a sixth-generation fighter monopoly for the Pentagon, after it was also selected last year to provide the US Air Force’s next combat aircraft, dubbed F-47.

The generational labelling has been used for about 35 years since the Lockheed YF-22 and Northrop YF-23 battled it out in 1991 to be the US Air Force’s first fifth-generation fighter.

Compared to the previous generation of fighters which included the F/A-18, F-15, and F-16, fifth generation included stealthy shaping and coatings, integrated avionics and sensors, the ability to cruise supersonically without using fuel-hungry afterburners, and the internal carriage of weapons.

The F-35 which evolved out of the Joint Strike Fighter (JSF) program is also labelled as a fifth-generation combat aircraft, as are China’s J-20 and J-35, and Russia’s Su-57 fighters. China has also revealed a couple of newer aircraft designs in the past year dubbed J-36 and J-50, but little is known about these yet.

To be labelled as sixth generation, it is generally accepted that the F-47 and F/A-XX will add AI-assisted processing, additional stealth features such as a lack of vertical tails, new more efficient engines, and the capability to control multiple collaborative combat aircraft (CCA) in flight. It is also expected the new aircraft will be somewhat larger and have far greater range than those they will replace.

The selection of Boeing for F/A-XX means it is likely it and the F-47 will share many design features, components, and capabilities, as observers have previously said it would be beyond a single company’s capability to concurrently develop two sixth-generation combat aircraft.

Boeing also continues to manufacture advanced variants of the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and F-15EX Eagle for the US Navy, US Air Force, and other countries, as well as the new MQ-25 Stingray uncrewed carrier-borne refuelling aircraft.

F/A-XX concept art. Image: Boeing.

The F/A-XX will replace US Navy Super Hornets. Photo: US Navy.

F-47 concept art. Image: Boeing.

Boeing beat out Northrop Grumman for F/A-XX, while Lockheed Martin failed to be shortlisted last year. But Northrop Grumman is busy developing and producing the B-21 bomber for the US Air Force as well as fuselage components for the F-35, while Lockheed Martin continues to struggle to roll out upgrades for its F-35 program.

Both Northrop Grumman and Lockheed Martin have been reported to also have a number of smaller highly classified intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) aircraft programs also in development.

The F/A-XX contract is valued at US$20bn (A$29bn), and covers the full-scale development phase including multiple test aircraft for ground, airworthiness, systems and, weapons integration testing. Production contracts will follow. The aircraft will be manufactured in St Louis, and will be powered by General Electric engines.

Its primary role will be long-range strike missions against targets in heavily defended airspace, and will also be tasked with defending aircraft carriers and other high-value assets from air and missile attacks.

Michael Duffey, the Pentagon’s Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment said the F/A-XX was a critical pillar for the US Navy.

“F/A-XX will dominate contested airspace, extend operational reach, and deliver a decisive combat advantage for the warfighter,” he said.

“The F/A-XX platform represents a crucial, non-negotiable investment in America’s national security and long-term air combat capabilities.”

Australian-born president and CEO of Boeing Defense, Space & Security, Steve Parker said it was an honour to be selected to produce the Navy’s first sixth-generation platform.

“Backed by decades of work, bolstered by game-changing innovations and solidified by the investments we’ve made in new facilities uniquely suited to build multiple products with next-generation capabilities, our dedicated and talented team is ready to execute this critical program,” he said.

“Delivering two advanced fighters in parallel was always our plan, and we invested accordingly.

“We are ready and able to build multiple concurrent future combat aircraft franchise programs.”

Both the F/A-XX and F-47 programs likely point to what the Royal Australian Air Force will be operating in the future, with a decision on the replacement of the RAAF’s F/A-18F Super Hornets and EA-18G Growlers scheduled to be made in the early-to-mid-2030s, for service entry around 2040.

Original Article published by Andrew McLaughlin on PS News.

canberra.title: Medicinal cannabis driving reform hits roadblock as government says technology isn’t ready
canberra.snippet: Canberra’s medicinal cannabis users face a longer wait for protection from drug-driving laws, with the ACT Government arguing a surge in ...
canberra.content:
Unlike alcohol, there is no agreed THC threshold that police can use to determine when someone is too impaired to drive. Photo: ACT Policing.

Canberra’s medicinal cannabis users face a longer wait for protection from drug-driving laws, with the ACT Government arguing a surge in prescriptions and the lack of a reliable roadside impairment test make reform too risky for now.

But the government has not closed the door completely, conceding that detecting THC is not the same as proving a driver is impaired and suggesting better technology could eventually clear the way for change.

The issue was at the centre of an Assembly inquiry into ACT Greens Deputy Leader and transport spokesperson Andrew Braddock’s Road Transport (Alcohol and Drugs) Amendment Bill 2026, introduced earlier this year.

The Bill seeks to provide a defence for medicinal cannabis patients who test positive for THC after legally using their prescribed medication, while retaining offences for driving while impaired.

Currently, a prescription does not provide a defence if THC is detected in a driver’s system.

Health Minister Marisa Paterson pointed to the rapid growth in medicinal cannabis prescriptions as one reason the government was reluctant to change that approach.

The inquiry heard there were about 56,000 prescribing events involving about 10,600 ACT patients between June 2024 and June 2026.

Dr Paterson said the growth of telehealth prescribing also meant patients could receive medicinal cannabis from someone other than their regular GP, who may not have access to their complete medical history.

But Attorney-General Tara Cheyne acknowledged one of the key arguments made by supporters of reform.

“We can all appreciate … that presence and detection of THC is not the same as impairment,” she said.

Unlike alcohol, however, there is no agreed THC threshold that police can use to determine when someone is too impaired to drive.

Ms Cheyne said THC could affect people differently and current roadside testing could detect its presence but could not provide sufficient certainty about impairment.

She rejected suggestions the government was taking a “zero tolerance” approach, saying it recognised people had legitimate medical reasons for using cannabis.

“I absolutely think there’s a technology answer to this,” she said.

“It’s just we’re not there yet.”

ACT Policing backed the cautious approach, warning that drugs could affect concentration, reaction times and a person’s ability to safely control a vehicle.

ACT Chief Police Officer Scott Lee said moving away from presence-based testing would leave officers with the difficult task of assessing impairment at the roadside.

Signs such as slightly slower reactions, reduced concentration or poorer decision-making might not be immediately obvious, and Deputy Commissioner Lee said expanding impairment testing would require significant additional training and resources.

Mr Braddock challenged why medicinal cannabis patients should face a presence-based offence when drivers taking prescription opioids and other potentially impairing medications do not.

Police said officers could still act where they suspected someone was impaired by another drug. If roadside alcohol and drug screening returned negative results but there were reasonable grounds to suspect impairment, a driver could be taken for a blood test and toxicological evidence could be used to support a driving-under-the-influence charge.

Mr Braddock said evidence from medicinal cannabis advocates and medical and public-health organisations showed the ACT could learn from other approaches rather than leave patients with the status quo.

“No one should drive whilst impaired and my bill doesn’t change that,” he said.

“Patients taking medicinal cannabis are extremely low risk and we heard evidence that common driving distractions such as listening to the radio pose a much higher road safety risk.”

The inquiry also considered whether any new defence should extend to learner and provisional drivers and heavy-vehicle operators.

Police pointed to NSW, where some categories of drivers are excluded, and argued the ACT should consider similar safeguards.

The government has also questioned the Bill’s retrospective provisions. ACT Policing has not historically recorded whether cannabis detected in a driver’s system was legally prescribed, which could make earlier cases difficult to reassess.

canberra.title: Prosecution of alleged Chinese spy ring suffers major blow
canberra.snippet: The prosecution of an alleged Chinese spy ring has suffered a major blow as prosecutors have dropped all of the allegations made against ...
canberra.content:
30 September 2026

Siru Zheng (centre) is the only one out of her two co-defendants, a man and the first woman arrested, who can legally be named. Photos: AFP/Albert McKnight.

The prosecution of an alleged Chinese spy ring has suffered a major blow as prosecutors have dropped all of the allegations made against one of the trio.

Three Chinese nationals were accused of spying on Guan Yin Citta Dharma Door for the Chinese Government. Region has previously obtained court documents outlining the allegations against them.

When the first woman was arrested in 2025, it was the first time in Australia that a person had been charged with foreign interference that involved targeting members of the community.

She and a man charged over the allegations legally cannot be identified, while the third person alleged to have made up their trio of spies was 32-year-old Siru Zheng.

All three pleaded not guilty to reckless foreign interference, and the case has slowly been making its way through the ACT Magistrates Court.

But on Wednesday (30 September), the court heard that prosecutors were withdrawing the charge laid against the man.

“That’s effectively the end of the proceedings for him,” said barrister Anthony Williamson SC, who represented all three defendants.

In court documents, police said they raided the man’s home in December 2025. He then allegedly admitted that the first woman had sent him several questions about Guan Yin Citta and that he had collated 99 gigabytes of data about the movement before sending it to her.

While the withdrawal of his charge is a major change to the overall allegations, prosecutors are still pursuing the first woman and Ms Zheng.

In fact, the court heard that the first woman had been handed a new charge of intentional foreign interference.

The prosecutor asked to adjourn the case against the pair as there was still outstanding material for the brief of evidence.

Mr Williamson said he was happy to give prosecutors as long as they needed to file the remainder of the evidence, as he did not want the matter to keep returning to court only to be adjourned again.

Magistrate Ian Temby adjourned the matter to 12 December, but he also urged authorities to “get their skates on” as he said there shouldn’t be any more adjournments.

The magistrate also ordered all the legal costs to be paid for the man. In addition, he ordered legal costs for the latest adjournment to be paid for the first woman and Ms Zheng.

Bail has been continued for the two remaining defendants.

The first woman’s name had been suppressed out of concern that publishing it could prejudice her case, while the man’s name was suppressed on national security grounds.

canberra.title: Canberra founders competing with tech giants win top entrepreneurship award
canberra.snippet: The Canberra innovators who created tech solutions to rival Microsoft, Google and Amazon have received the ACT’s premier regional t...
canberra.content:
ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr presented the Pearcey Foundation ACT Chief Minister’s Entrepreneur Award to Trellis Data founders Rachel and Michael Gately. Photo: Andrew Barr/LinkedIn.

The Canberra innovators who created tech solutions to rival Microsoft, Google and Amazon have received the ACT’s premier regional tech-entrepreneurship accolade.

Trellis Data co-founders Rachel and Michael Gately were presented with the 2026 ACT Chief Minister’s Pearcey Entrepreneur Award by the Pearcey Foundation in recognition of their major contribution to the Australian ICT industry, particularly in building Australia’s sovereign AI capability.

The husband-and-wife team established Trellis Data in Canberra in 2016 to address a major market vulnerability: the reliance of Australian government, defence and enterprise organisations on foreign, cloud-dependent AI platforms that compromise data sovereignty, privacy and operational security.

The Gatelys set out to build a secure, fully sovereign platform to support a wide range of data sources and machine learning models. It would compete directly with tech behemoths like Microsoft, Google and Amazon.

“Trellis Data has the talent and the ability, and it would just be an opportunity missed for Australia for us not to devote our time and resources and efforts to create a truly sovereign AI capability,” Rachel said.

“It’s been our vision from the start to build those high-security sovereign AI solutions. We’ve really believed that it’s something Australia needed, and believed that Australia would back us in those endeavours.

“We can see a future where Canberra is a technology hub, but not just that, we see it as a place where top talent congregates to solve the hard problems.”

After 10 years, Trellis Data now stands as a flagship Australian AI success story.

The company created one of the world’s fastest speech-to-text and translation algorithms, capable of operating in air-gapped, high-security environments.

Earlier this year, Trellis Data also launched Agentaus, a publicly accessible, fully sovereign, defence-grade AI platform where all model inference, data storage and processing occur within secure Australian data centres.

Today, Trellis Data provides critical capability that ensures sensitive national security, intelligence and health data remain fully protected on home soil.

However, taking on global giants was not without massive operational and capital challenges.

The Gatelys had to develop proprietary neural network architectures from scratch, convince risk-averse public sector buyers to adopt local deep-tech solutions and recruit top-tier machine learning engineers from Canberra’s highly competitive talent market.

They also had to fund aggressive R&D cycles while maintaining strict compliance with stringent government security accreditations.

ACT Pearcey Foundation Chair Dr Tim Turner highlighted the courage it took for the Gatelys to commit their personal and financial capital to challenge global tech titans.

“They chose to fund independent proprietary development rather than building wrappers around international AI models, so that public sector agencies can safely leverage AI without compromising security,” he said.

“Most importantly, Rachel and Michael have shown us that world-class AI software can be conceptualised, built, and commercially scaled out of Canberra. Their success offers a powerful example for other Australian technology founders pursuing high-growth deep-tech models.”

Today, the company boasts a compound annual revenue growth rate of over 100 per cent, rapid expansion into international markets like the United States, and widespread deployment across major Australian federal departments, law enforcement agencies and defence programs.

The Pearcey Award acknowledges individuals who demonstrate outstanding innovation, success and leadership in ICT entrepreneurship, celebrating local achievement while bolstering Canberra’s entrepreneurial ecosystem.

“This was an incredible recognition of the work we’ve achieved to date, and it felt like a clear affirmation that what we’re doing at Trellis Data is making a tangible difference,” Rachel said.

Rachel and Michael Gately will represent the Territory at the national Pearcey Awards in November.

canberra.title: Shoebridge trumps Hanson-Young and Faruqi to be new Greens leader
canberra.snippet: David Shoebridge has been elected the new Greens leader, following this week’s shock resignation of Larissa Waters. In a three-way contes...
canberra.content:
NSW Senator David Shoebridge is the new Greens leader, following a three-way contest in a party room ballot. Photo: John Lomnicki.

David Shoebridge has been elected the new Greens leader, following this week’s shock resignation of Larissa Waters.

In a three-way contest for the leadership, Senator Shoebridge knocked both Mehreen Faruqi and Sarah Hanson-Young out of the race in a party room ballot on Wednesday (30 September).

The New South Wales senator ran on a joint ticket with Victorian senator Steph Hodgins-May, who was subsequently elected deputy leader.

In the leadership contest, Senator Hanson-Young was eliminated in the first round after receiving only two votes, and the second round saw Senator Shoebridge win seven votes to Senator Faruqi’s four.

Senator Hodgins-May defeated WA senator Jordan Steele-John and Tasmanian senator Vanessa Bleyer for the deputy position.

The new leader praised Senator Waters’ work in the top job and said the Greens do not want to improve the Labor Party but to replace it as a party of government.

“We present this fresh, new, strong face to build on the amazing work of Larissa and the team,” he said.

“We are not here to manage a broken system. We are here to replace it.”

A lawyer and campaigner, Senator Shoebridge has represented workers, challenged attempts to restrict workers’ compensation, and advocated for survivors of child sexual abuse.

He was a Greens member of the NSW State Parliament before being elected to the Senate.

“Now is the time to build the Greens as the home for every Australian who wants action on the climate crisis, a fair return from our resources, a secure home and income, and to not sell out our independence to the US or the 1 per cent,” he said on Wednesday.

“The economy isn’t working for people. Millions of Australians can see that something is fundamentally wrong when people working full time can’t afford a home while billionaires get richer and big corporations buy off politicians.

“We want to build an Australia where your bank balance, your postcode or where you were born do not determine the life you get to live.

“Whether it’s in parliament, estimates, or leading the movement, the Greens will take on corporate power, defend your rights, rebuild strong public institutions and stop politicians from selling you out …

“Labor has proven they can’t stop One Nation because they made the conditions for them to thrive. The Greens can.”

Former Greens leader Larissa Waters and new Greens deputy leader Steph Hodgins-May. Photo: Steph Hodgins-May Facebook.

Senator Hodgins-May is an environmental lawyer who worked with the United Nations and Greenpeace before entering parliament.

“My generation has grown up seeing politicians sell out our future for corporate greed – delaying action on climate change while housing, childcare and the basic things people need to build a good life become harder and harder to afford,” she said on her election as deputy leader.

“Rich corporations are screwing us over because Labor, Liberals and One Nation are letting them write the rules.

“We’re not here to reform Labor, we’re here to replace them.

“We need to give people hope that a better future is possible.”

Other members of the Greens’ new leadership team are Tasmanian Senator Nick McKim as party whip; Senator Hanson-Young (South Australia) as manager of Greens business; and Queensland Senator Penny Allman-Payne as party room chair and deputy whip.

Senator Faruqi (NSW) ran on a joint ticket with Senator McKim, but she did not nominate for the deputy’s role herself after being defeated in the leaders’ ballot.

She issued a statement after the vote expressing her disappointment and called for party rules to be changed so the entire membership votes for the leadership.

But she added she was as “inspired as ever by the fierce dedication” of Greens members around the country.

“Of course, I am disappointed the party room chose another direction, and know many others will feel the same way,” she said.

“I did not stand for deputy leader today because, on reflection, I believe I can best play my part in that action outside the constraints of the leadership team.

“I’ve long advocated publicly that Greens leaders should be elected by members with enough time for thoughtful deliberation on who is best to grow our party.

“I share members’ frustration that the opposite happened this week.

“Without a member vote, we cannot call ourselves a grassroots party. I call on the new leadership team to set a timeline for one member, one vote.”

Georgie Dent’s National Press Club address recently went viral after she laid bare the compounding pressures on modern families. Between skyrocketing cost of living, rigid workplace expectations, and an eye-watering gap between school days and work hours, is the current system setting parents up to fail? australia.content:
Police appeal for information after serious ebike crash in Sydney’s south

Officials said emergency services were called to the suburb of Engadine about 3.30pm amid reports a child had been struck by an ebike rider. A five-year-old boy was treated at the scene by paramedics for serious leg injuries before he was taken to Sydney children’s hospital. He is in stable condition.

Officers were told the e-bike rider did not stop and left the scene before police arrived. They are searching for two people in relation to the incident.

Anyone with information related to the crash has been urged to contact police.

    Welcome

What we learned, Wednesday 30 September

That’s a wrap on our live coverage, before we go let’s recap the day’s top headlines:

  • NSW senator David Shoebridge has become the new Greens leader, replacing Larissa Waters. Steph Hodgins-May has been named deputy leader.

  • Inflation has jumped to 4% in the year to August, from 3.5%, as underlying price pressures remained stubbornly high amid worries the Reserve Bank may have to hike again.

  • Anthony Albanese and Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, announced early works are beginning on the second stage of the long-awaited train line to Melbourne airport – a 7.6km stretch of the train line from Albion to Keilor East.

  • OpenAI’s Medicare breach has prompted a government-wide assessment of cyber systems to bolster Australia’s public sector against further AI threats.

  • Two men and a teenage boy have been charged in relation to the alleged mistaken identity shooting of Sydney student Marco Tapia – including the person who allegedly held the gun – police say.

  • A man has been charged with murder after the deaths of two men at Gurranang, about 25km north of Grafton in northern New South Wales, police said.

  • ABC’s finance titan Alan Kohler will retire at the end of this year, capping a three decade-tenure at the national broadcaster.

  • Laneway festival dropped its lineup for next year’s event, and there are some heavy hitters from both the international scene and Australian shores.

Thanks for sticking around, we’ll see you tomorrow!

‘I am ready to play hardball’: Hodgins-May vows to take drastic change in new role

Newly appointed Greens deputy leader Steph Hodgins-May said the role presented an opportunity to “reimagine what the future could look like if we put people ahead of those corporate profiteers”.

Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, she said she was determined to represent Australians calling for greater action from the government.

I am ready to play hardball … I’m listening to the Victorians, the Australians who are every day telling me they are distraught at the fact that this government is not doing more to help people.

Incremental change doesn’t cut it when we are staring down the biggest El Niño on record, and the potential for immense droughts, floods, fires. Incrementalism won’t cut it on climate action. Incrementalism won’t cut it when we want to materially make lives better, so we are demanding more ambition and courage from the Labor party, but not expecting it.

Hodgins-May said she would “take that responsibility incredibly seriously”.

If that means playing hardball with the ALP and the Labor government, then absolutely. But if they turn around tomorrow and say, ‘Hang on, maybe we can do things differently,’ and serve us up some reforms that will genuinely change lives for the better, then I’m all ears and ready to go. We are ready to go as a team.

Commbank becomes first of big four banks to increase home loan rates

Commonwealth Bank has announced it will increase variable home loan interest rates by 0.25% per annum following Tuesday’s RBA rate hike.

The changes will take effect from 9 October 2026.

CBA Executive of Retail Banking Angus Sullivan said:

Each customer’s circumstances are different, and our teams are ready to provide support, help them understand their options and consider what might work best for their situation.

For some customers, the immediate priority might be understanding how their repayments and budget may change and where adjustments can be made. For others, it may be having a more detailed conversation with us about their finances.

Peugeot announces major recall of over 500 cars due to ‘software issue’

The European car brand has recalled hundreds of vehicles in Australia over a “software issue” that could increase the “risk of serious injury or death”.

A warning published on the Department for Transport’s website said the fault could cause the interior door handles to deactivate unexpectedly while the engine was running.

The issue may prevent passengers from opening the doors from inside the vehicle, potentially leaving them unable to escape in an emergency.

Peugeot estimated that 550 vehicles manufactured in 2024 and 2025 were affected.

Owners of affected vehicles are being urged to contact their local dealership to have the software updated at no cost.

NSW’s Greens condemn state government’s extension approval of Hunter Valley Operations coalmine expansions

The party has criticised the state government’s planning commission for approving the proposal.

The approval will allow Glencore and Yancoal’s Hunter Valley Operations to continue until 2045. The Greens said the mine will produce an estimated 809m tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent – about seven times NSW’s annual emissions.

Greens climate and energy spokesperson, Cate Faehrmann, said the decision had “killed any chance of NSW meeting its own climate emissions reduction targets”.

Each year, the Minns government falls further and further behind on reaching its net zero targets. The latest report from July shows that NSW is not set to reach its 2030 target until 2034 and its 2035 target until 2042.

The Minns Labor government doesn’t care about climate action. It prefers propping up a dying industry, with even the International Energy Agency saying that global demand will decline from 2030.

The signs of climate breakdown caused by the burning of fossil fuels are all around us and we’re facing a super El Niño here this summer. Meanwhile, the Minns government’s love affair with coal continues.

Police investigate public fights at SA beaches

South Australian police are investigating after reports of public fights at beaches.

The possible move comes after “several disturbances along the metropolitan coastline late yesterday”, including reports of fighting at Glenelg and Henley Beach.

Detective said it’s understood a small number of individuals were involved in public fights as several young people spectated.

Police said they were alerted to the incidents through social media videos. They said no reports had yet been made to police and no injuries had been reported.

Officers are working to identify and locate those involved.

The force’s annual Operation Jericho monitors crime, public disorder and road safety along Adelaide’s coastline during summer.

Achol Arok

Good afternoon!

Thanks for sticking around, I’ll be taking the reins for the rest of the arvo.

Nick Visser

That’s all from me. Achol Arok will take the blog from here. Enjoy your Wednesday.

Trump’s man in Canberra starts work

Tom McIlroy

The new American ambassador to Australia, David Brat, has begun the new job, after presenting his diplomatic credentials to the governor general on Tuesday.

Brat met Sam Mostyn at a ceremony at Government House in Canberra.

The US embassy says Brat’s priorities in Australia include deepening the defence relationship, advancing the Aukus nuclear submarines pact, strengthening cooperation on critical minerals, and expanding trade and investment.

In his first official act, Brat paid tribute to Australian servicemen and women by laying a wreath at the Australian War Memorial.

“Australia has been our closest ally and friend for generations. It’s an honour to visit such an awe-inspiring tribute as Ambassador,” he said.

US and Australian soldiers have fought side-by-side and stood shoulder-to-shoulder for decades in times of war and times of peace. I look forward to furthering our longstanding defence partnership during my posting to Australia.

He said he looked forward to meeting Australians, including sport fans.

“Both of our nations are crazy about sports, and I can’t wait to get out there, whether it’s tennis, NRL, AFL, rugby, or cricket,” he said.

Mother of Marco Tapia wants people to remember her son ‘beyond the circumstances of his death’

Claudia Tapia, the mother of Marco Tapia, the Sydney student mistakenly killed in an alleged crime hit gone wrong, has released a statement after her son’s death.

NSW police said earlier two men and a teenage boy had been charged in the shooting with a series of offences, including murder. A NSW official alleged the trio were “hired guns” by organised crime groups to commit the shooting, saying Tapia was a “completely innocent party”.

Claudia Tapia said her family was “so grateful to NSW Police and everyone continuing to work on this investigation”. She went on:

For our family, however, every development brings us back to the reality that Marco is no longer here. We want people to know who Marco was beyond the circumstances of his death.

Marco was a warm, caring and loving 23 years old, a biomedical engineering student, a committed Christian, a youth leader, a volunteer, a martial artist, a boyfriend, a brother and our deeply loved son. …

Marco had plans. He had purpose. He had a future, and he was already making a difference in the lives of others. His death is part of his story, but it must never become his identity. Marco was not simply a victim. He was our son, a brother, a boyfriend, a friend, a man of faith, a young leader and a biomedical engineer in the making, who was going to impact this sphere greatly.

Antarctic winter sea ice falls to third-lowest level on record as scientists warn of ‘now problem’

Antarctica’s winter sea ice has peaked at its third-lowest level on record, falling 1m sq km short of the long-term average, scientists have confirmed.

Confirmation of the peak meant the four lowest years on record for the continent’s sea ice – a vital component of the planet’s climate and critical for marine life – had all occurred in the past four years.

Satellites have been watching the continent’s sea ice since 1979, and this year data showed the sea ice peaked on 14 September at 17.59m sq km, about 1m sq km short of the average maximum, or an area roughly twice the size of Spain.

Read more here:

australia.title: David Shoebridge wants the Greens to ‘seize this moment’. Is his more combative style the answer?
australia.snippet: New leader says his party must connect with millions of disaffected voters and ‘make them believe in politics again’ Follow our Australia...
australia.content:
As One Nation’s polling surged this year, and Pauline Hanson ate away at the votes of first the Coalition and then Labor, one curious mainstay emerged; the Greens remained seemingly anchored to the 10-12% range, no matter which poll you look at.

That’s despite the fact that, arguably, there’s rarely been more fertile political ground for the Greens leader to reap rewards; a centrist Labor government with a big majority but increasingly on the nose, a resurgent anti-immigration populist party backed by Australia’s richest mining billionaire, a Coalition in disarray, a cost-of-living crisis set ablaze by rising interest rates and inflation, and a public increasingly alarmed about the nexus of big tech, big datacentres and shadowy AI oligarchs operating with impunity.

David Shoebridge, in his first comments as the new Greens leader, seemed to acknowledge the party should, and could, be doing better.

“The Greens need to seize this moment because politics demands it of us,” he said.

“This is an extraordinary moment in politics, and we can all feel it. We can feel that politics as usual is not providing the answers that people are desperately calling for now.”

Moments after winning Wednesday’s party-room ballot, Shoebridge, a former corporate lawyer, councillor from Woollahra in Sydney’s affluent eastern suburbs and state upper house MP, signalled he would take a more combative approach to not only One Nation, but the government as well. He argued the Greens were “not here to reform the Labor party. We are here to replace the Labor party.”

Arguably a message about cost of living should resonate better when it comes from a party that didn’t receive a private plane as a gift.

Progressives in Australia have been buoyed up by the successes of socialist outsider candidates in the US and UK, but there have been quiet frustrations inside the Greens that they haven’t managed to emulate the likes of Zohran Mamdani, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Zack Polanski in the United Kingdom.

Shoebridge says the Greens must both fill a “vacuum” left by Labor and “recognise” the factors driving disaffected voters to Hanson.

“Our task in this moment is to connect with those millions of Australians who have quite legitimate and real anger with politics, and make them believe in politics again, and not believe in the politics of hate and division,” he said.

Another task, of course, is internal. The Greens usually decide leaders by consensus, but Shoebridge won a rare contested party-room vote. He saw off challenges from Mehreen Faruqi and Sarah Hanson-Young, initially winning six of 11 votes. Shoebridge was last to publicly declare his hand, and the optics of a white man besting two women more experienced in federal politics will surely be dissected by some in the party.

Faruqi, shortly after the result was decided, said she was “disappointed the party chose another direction” and claimed “many others will feel the same way”. She said ordinary party members felt “frustration” the leadership was decided by politicians, not grassroots membership; Shoebridge earlier had said he supported grassroots involvement in choosing leaders, and will be held to this.

He also will preside over a critical period of renewal for the Greens, with the veteran senator Peter Whish-Wilson already having left parliament, and South Australian senator Barbara Pocock not contesting the next election.

There is a push on from some in the party’s more activist ranks for those spots to be given to younger, digitally savvy, vigorous campaigners in the mould of the US “democratic socialist” movement.

One key point to look out for is Shoebridge’s strategy for negotiating with Labor on legislation. Bandt campaigned at the 2022 election on pushing Labor to go further, but government sources pinned his unexpected defeat in 2025 on the Greens playing hardball on housing legislation. Larissa Waters took a more constructive approach, seeming more open to negotiations. Judging from past performance, and his pledge to “replace” not “reform” Labor, Shoebridge may take the tougher line.

Waters is well-liked, both among colleagues and more broadly across federal politics, seen as more conciliatory and pragmatic than some in her party room. There was genuine remorse and upset in the Greens as she stood down from the leadership to focus on managing a chronic kidney issue, and she must be given ample credit for holding the party together after the unexpected losses of leader Adam Bandt and rising stars Max Chandler-Mather and Stephen Bates at the 2025 election.

On a personal level, it must be acknowledged Shoebridge is not the most popular guy across the parliament or among Labor types, but much of that stems from his relentless style of questioning, needling and interrogation of political opponents and government officials.

Politico reported last week that the government offered the Greens a spot on a new AI committee, but with the proviso that it couldn’t be Shoebridge; clips of him forensically drawing answers out of public servants on Aukus, AI and the bureaucracy have gone viral online.

As one Greens source said: “He does act like the smartest guy in the room, but often, he actually is.”

Or as the Liberal senator James Paterson told the Guardian in 2025: “David Shoebridge and I don’t agree on much, but he’s easily the most effective Green and one of the most impactful crossbenchers in the Senate.”

With parliament returning in mid-October, it won’t be long before we see how effective he can be as leader.

australia.title: Approval of biggest coal project in NSW planning commission’s history described as ‘infamous betrayal’
australia.snippet: Independent Planning Commission says climate change impacts from Hunter Valley project will be ‘outweighed’ by economic benefits Follow o...
australia.content:
The New South Wales independent planner has approved the biggest coalmine project to ever go before it, allowing mining to continue until 2045 at a Hunter Valley project described by climate groups as a “carbon bomb”.

The Independent Planning Commission (IPC) has greenlit the Hunter Valley Operations (HVO) Continuation Project after a contentious assessment that drew in climate and environment groups, unions, state authorities and more than 10,000 public submissions.

On Wednesday, the commission said the greenhouse gas emissions from the mine, near Singleton, would “contribute to climate change impacts on the people, economy and environment of the Hunter region, NSW and globally”.

But these impacts had been “outweighed by its benefits to the Hunter region and NSW, including continued employment, economic activity, support for local business, ongoing royalties and taxation revenue”.

The IPC said the decision would “provide economic stability for the Hunter region and support a more orderly transition for workers, businesses and communities as the coal industry changes over time”.

In response, Georgina Woods, the co-national coordinator of the Lock the Gate Alliance, said: “There is no other way to describe this other than a catastrophic failure of the New South Wales planning system to protect the people of the state from the worst impacts of global warming.”

Climate campaigners had strongly opposed the project, saying it was out of line with Australia’s commitments under the Paris climate agreement and could affect extreme weather events.

‘Infamous betrayal of the public trust’

Groups reacted with dismay at the approval, with Rising Tide describing it as the “largest climate policy failure in NSW history”.

The Climate Council had described the project as a “climate bomb that would supercharge climate disasters”. One of its councillors – the former NSW Fire and Rescue commissioner Greg Mullins – on Wednesday raised concerns over overseas emissions from the coal.

“What NSW exports as coal, we import back as bushfires, floods, heatwaves and droughts,” Mullins said. “Climate harm does not stop at the border, and neither does the responsibility for it.”

Woods said the process for considering fossil fuel projects in NSW was “the best in the country” – including with its climate change act and an independent and transparent planning authority.

“The law was in place, and I am frankly shocked. It will go down in history as an infamous betrayal of the public trust.”

Glencore and Yancoal – the joint owners of HVO – want to continue digging coal at the north mine site until 2045, and mine from 2030 to 2042 at the south mine.

The IPC said HVO would have to prepare a plan to manage the emissions from burning the coal overseas that would limit exports to “jurisdictions with greenhouse gas emissions policies consistent with the goals of the Paris Agreement”.

The project also requires federal environmental approval – a process expected to be decided before the end of the year.

HVO said coal had been mined at the site for 75 years and the project, which it said had strong local support, provided jobs for 1,500 people.

The state’s independent Net Zero Commission had warned the planning commission that approving the project could affect the state’s ability to meet climate targets in the future.

Over the life of the project, the company has estimated that 809m tonnes of CO2-equivalent will be released into the atmosphere.

About 794Mt of that will be emitted when the coal is burned overseas, 87% of which will come from power plants, according to presentations HVO made to the IPC.

The Net Zero Commission recommended the planning authority should consider all of the impacts from the mine’s greenhouse gases, including from the burning of the coal in power stations overseas, and pointed to advances in climate science that can attribute real-world impacts to fossil fuel projects.

A new tool released by climate scientists this week suggested the additional global heating caused by the project’s approval would expose almost half a million people to unprecedented heat, kill nearly 15 million coral colonies on the Great Barrier Reef every time it bleaches and lead to more than 100 additional deaths from heatwaves in Europe to the end of this century.

The NSW Nature Conservation Council’s chief executive, Jacqui Mumford, said the decision was Chris Minns’ “biggest climate failure” as premier and highlighted the government’s “complete inability to appropriately respond to the ever-growing climate crisis”.

The NSW state Greens MP Sue Higginson said the approval was an “absolute betrayal of the science”, saying she “wouldn’t be surprised if the decision is challenged in the courts”.

HVO said the approval “marked a pivotal milestone for 1,500 mine workers, their families and the regional economy”.

It said the company was engaging with the national environmental protection agency to secure federal approval “by the end of December 2026 to continue operations”.

The NSW Minerals Council urged the state government to pass legislation to limit the opportunity for a “legal challenge from climate activists determined to object to every coal mining approval on ideological grounds”.

australia.title: NSW man accused of murdering neighbour – and then murdering his relative two weeks later
australia.snippet: Police allege Nicholas Scott killed 79-year-old then ‘set upon’ 59-year-old relative who arrived at Gurranang to sort out estate Follow o...
australia.content:
A man accused of murdering two members of a family on the same property a fortnight apart has faced court.

The body of a 59-year-old man was found by police on Monday afternoon in a shed on a property at Gurranang, about 25km north of Grafton in northern New South Wales.

The discovery was made as police combed the address for clues two weeks after a 79-year-old man’s body was found inside a home on the property.

Det Supt Joe Doueihi on Wednesday said the alleged murder victims were related, adding the younger man came to NSW to help police with their investigation and to sort out the 79-year-old’s estate.

He alleged the 59-year-old was “set upon” by a neighbour when he went to his deceased relative’s property.

“It’s absolutely shocking for that family and for that community,” the homicide squad commander told reporters.

Police alleged the neighbour – 32-year-old Nicholas Scott – was responsible for both murders.

Scott was arrested at a hospital in Grafton, where he was receiving treatment, at about midday on Tuesday.

He was taken to Grafton police station where he was charged with two counts of murder and stealing a motor vehicle.

Scott briefly appeared in court on Wednesday morning and did not apply for bail.

He will remain behind bars before returning to court in December.

Supt Joanne Schultz told reporters on Tuesday the scene was extremely confronting and traumatic for first responders.

“[Police] had attended the property to make further inquiries, they did not anticipate what they found,” she said.

Police believe the 59-year-old man died in the past 24 to 48 hours, two weeks after police first came to the rural acreage to investigate the older man’s death.

“The scene was not maintained for the entirety of that time,” Supt Schultz said.

The deceased men appeared to have suffered similar injuries.

Strike Force Faneel continues to investigate the deaths.

world.title: Burundi agrees to receive ‘third-country’ migrant deportees from US
world.snippet: Burundi joins several other African nations in accepting people deported under Trump’s hardline policy Burundi has agreed to join a clutc...
world.content:
Burundi has agreed to join a clutch of ⁠other African nations in receiving migrants from other countries deported from the US under ⁠Donald Trump’s hardline ⁠immigration ​policy.

However, the authorities in Bujumbura, the country’s economic capital, said Burundi will only accept those not accused of crime or terrorism links, said ⁠Nancy Ninette Mutoni, a spokesperson for the country’s president, Évariste Ndayishimiye. Tuesday’s announcement gave no details of numbers, timing or financial ⁠details.

Washington has sent so-called “third-country deportees” to some half ​a dozen African nations ‌as well as many other countries, often where they have no ties, have never been and find themselves detained indefinitely, under opaque deals ‌that Senate Democrats say have cost tens of millions of ‌dollars.

In many cases, deportees had secured legal protections from immigration courts in the US against repatriation. But rights groups say the third-country deals allow the US to circumvent those protections.

Mutoni said preparations were underway to arrange accommodation, ‌living conditions and integration into local communities in Burundi. “Receiving them requires serious planning – where they will stay, what they ​will eat and how they will live alongside the local population,” she said.

“If they choose to join Burundian citizens and make a valuable contribution to national development, the law ⁠will be respected,” she said, regarding potential citizenship.

Burundi aimed ​to both ​strengthen diplomatic relations and provide ​hospitality to people in need, the spokesperson ​added.

The US ‌state department ​did not ​immediately respond to requests for comment while a spokesperson for the Burundi foreign ministry said details of the agreement were not yet available.

world.title: Top Trump figures push to direct human rights funding to rightwing causes
world.snippet: Support for white Afrikaners, anti-communism and others reveals how US redefining what qualifies as human rights With hours left before t...
world.content:
With hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a massive $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a campaign against Brazil’s supreme court, and programs that would reward ideological allies in Europe who protect “western civilisational norms”.

Critics have focused on 43 awards of a combined $176.9m that will bolster rightwing and conservative causes around the world while likely angering US allies over interference in internal politics. The Guardian has seen a sample of the controversial grants, which makes up most of the $205m in funding that Congress has appropriated for the entire human rights and democracy fund (HRDF).

Sources with knowledge of the grant process have told the Guardian that the awards were personally lobbied for by members of the Trump administration, and reflect interests that include JD Vance’s warnings of the collapse of traditional western values in Europe, and Stephen Miller’s push against immigration and to support white minorities in countries like South Africa.

“The story for me is the high-level – including White House-directed – attention on these programs,” said a person familiar with the discussions over the democracy awards. “These awards have been briefed at the highest levels of the department and have buy-in from the White House.”

The proposed awards represent a significant shift in US support for dissidents, human-rights defenders and civil-society groups under authoritarian governments. The new slate includes projects in wealthy nations, and focused on opposition to regulation, Brexit, migration, anti-communism, Christian protection and opposition to “gender ideology”, offering a window into how the Trump administration is redefining what qualifies as human rights and merits tens of millions of dollars in US foreign assistance.

“Congress appropriated money for the democracy fund on a bipartisan basis to support defenders of human rights, to assist victims of human rights violations and to instead promote the growth of democracy abroad,” said senator Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the US Senate committee on foreign relations.

“The Trump administration’s proposals would use taxpayer funds to promote far-right organizations and programs in established democracies. This is a waste of resources and undermines United States values and relations with democratic partners, including allies in Europe.”

The largest award of $40m was directed to a consortium led by the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation (VOC), an anti-communist non-profit that has received far smaller grants in the past. A state department vetting document seen by the Guardian records $96,997 in previous contracts in the last five years between the foundation and the department, all in the 2022 fiscal year, and notes that it had been vetted in 2019 in connection with tickets to the foundation’s gala. The vetting document also identifies Andrew Bremberg, a former Trump White House domestic policy adviser and US ambassador to the UN European office, as a “senior leader” of the foundation.

In July, ProPublica reported that Samuel Samson, a 27-year-old deputy assistant secretary overseeing the new grants, was linked to senior members of VOC through his studies at the Christian conservative Hillsdale College graduate program. (A state department official then told the outlet that the relationship had nothing to do with the grant).

Samson has described the US and Europe as partners in a shared civilizational struggle. Samson toured Austria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia last December – all countries that were floated to receive a $2m grant to counter migration weaponized by Russia and Belarus, and criticized NGOs that previous administrations had worked with for promoting what he called radical concepts, including gender theory and DEI.

The state department did not comment on individual grants but told the Guardian the programs were still in “active deliberation”, that awardees would meet guidelines for federal grants, and that all programming would undergo a “standard and rigorous vetting process by grant professionals.”

“Our programming in Europe aims to support our European allies in defending those rights and principles, along with their civilizational self-confidence and sovereignty from those who seek to undermine them,” a state department official said. “The national security strategy highlights our priorities in Europe which includes advancing political liberty, promoting free speech, and collaborating with European partners to jointly support European revitalization and civilizational self-confidence.”

Under the legislation authorizing the fund, the money must be assigned by 30 September, the end of the fiscal year, when unobligated funds typically lapse. Shaheen, the ranking member of the Senate foreign relations committee, has put a partial “hold” on giving the grants to some of the controversial awardees – setting up a showdown with the State Department with just hours left for the money to be obligated.

ProPublica first reported that Trump officials had drawn up at least a dozen no-bid grants aimed at rightwing and anti-immigration causes in Europe and advocates for white South Africans.

The document now shows how much of the fund the plan takes up, and which awards have since been dropped.

A $1m award titled “Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil” would fund civil society groups opposing what it calls judicial overreach and censorship by Brazil’s supreme court. The Trump administration sanctioned Justice Alexandre de Moraes last year after lobbying by Eduardo Bolsonaro, son of the former president.

A program titled “Promoting Western Civilization Allies” would be limited to implementers who do not subscribe to “ideologically weaponized accounts of human rights, such as gender ideology”, according to the document, and will receive $2m. It names possible recipients in Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and the Balkans with “anti-communist” and “natural rights” approaches.

One award was allocated to document “democratic backsliding” in Europe tied to “mass and illegal migration” and legislation by “supra-national entities”, while a $1m journalism consortium would push back against designations of “trusted” media outlets. The list also includes $2m for early-warning networks protecting Christians in Nigeria.

And a $3m no-bid award would go to the Jobs Foundation, a UK group run by Matthew Elliott, who led the Vote Leave campaign. The grant, titled “Countering Overregulation to Advance American Investment”, would promote a “common good capitalism index” and pro-business policy, including how the foundation promoted Brexit as a chance to cut the UK’s climate regulations.

The document also shows that a proposed $5m no-bid grant to the Free Speech Union, the British group founded by Toby Young, has been marked “withdrawn”. When the award was first reported in July, Young said the group had never applied for or received US government money (though Trump officials had reportedly met with the group during a European tour late last year).

The grant would have paid the group to campaign against online safety and hate speech laws, including Britain’s Online Safety Act, a law passed under the Conservatives in 2023. Meant to protect children from harmful content and is enforced by Ofcom, its age-verification rules – which took effect last year – have drawn constant criticism from the Trump administration, which cast them as censorship.

The Free Speech Union is the second British group to drop off the list. A $7m no-bid award to 878, a thinktank whose stated missions include restoring Judeo-Christian culture and “ending mass migration and deporting illegal immigrants”, was abandoned in July after pushback from Congress. It was founded by Jacob Rees-Mogg, who served as Brexit opportunities minister and business secretary before losing his seat at the 2024 election, and now presents on GB News.

The British awards would have sent $15m in US taxpayer money to groups run by two sitting Conservative peers and a former cabinet minister, on issues from online safety law to migration that are live in British politics.

world.title: DRC politician beaten to death after radio appearance about Ebola outbreak
world.snippet: Marie-Celestin Karondwa was attacked on Sunday after promoting measures to prevent spread of disease, his party says A senior member of t...
world.content:
A senior member of the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s ruling party was beaten to death on Sunday after appearing on a radio programme to raise awareness about the Ebola outbreak, a party representative has said.

Marie-Celestin Karondwa, the acting president of the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) party’s federal executive committee in Butembo, a new hotspot for the outbreak, was attacked after taking part in a ​radio show during which he ‌promoted prevention measures for the disease, ‌the UDPS federation in the city said in a statement, Reuters reported.

The party ‌said the attackers beat Karondwa, stole his belongings and set his house on fire, and that he later died from his injuries.

It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack, how many people were involved or what motivated it, but the party said Karondwa was “an innocent victim for having defended ‌the party’s position on the existence of the Ebola virus disease … and the threat it poses to ​the population”.

Karondwa’s death comes after a series of attacks on healthcare workers and treatment centres that experts say are fuelled by rumours and misinformation about the disease and distrust of health responders.

The incidents have included violence, riots and property damage and the disruption of essential services. On Saturday, ​armed men attacked a hand-washing ​checkpoint in the nearby Beni territory, killing at least one ​person and wounding ‌several others, a ​local civil ​society group reported.

First identified in 1976 in what is now the DRC, Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.

The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected 8,067 people and killed 3,901, according to data from the DRC’s health ministry.

Cases of the disease have been confirmed in seven provinces.

The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in the DRC’s history and second only ​globally to ​the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected ​more than ‌28,600 people ​and ​killed more than 11,000.

Data from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention shows the current outbreak has outpaced the west African one.

Last month, the World Health Organization warned it was on track to surpass the west Africa outbreak. Experts say the spread of the disease has been intensified by several factors, including conflict, aid cuts and the attacks on healthcare workers and treatment centres.

Reuters contributed to this report

world.title: At least 27 dead after two mass shootings in South Africa, police say
world.snippet: Seventeen people killed near Johannesburg in suspected ‘illegal goldmining turf war’, as 10 killed in separate incident at barbecue venue...
world.content:
Two separate mass shootings near South Africa’s two biggest cities killed at least 27 people, as the country grapples with one of the world’s highest murder rates amid investigations into corruption and criminality within the police.

The South African police service said on Sunday that 17 people were killed on Saturday night when eight suspects armed with AK-47 assault rifles and pistols opened fire at a bar in Wedela township, about 50 miles south-west of central Johannesburg. At least 15 other people sustained gunshot injuries in that attack, police said.

In a separate statement, police said 10 people had been killed in a mass shooting at an entertainment venue selling grilled meat, known as shisanyama, in Lwandle, near Cape Town. Another 11 people were wounded in that shooting. Police said they were searching for multiple suspects, without giving an exact number.

The two attacks happened days after a mass shooting by three gunmen at a house party near the east-coast city of Durban killed 11 people, including a pregnant woman.

No arrests had been made in the two latest mass shootings, police said.

South Africa has struggled with high rates of violent crime for years, but the series of mass shootings this week were shocking even to a country used to some of the highest violent crime rates in the world.

“This ​cannot go on like this,” South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, told local TV news channels. “This is the level of criminality that we must bring down, and our security forces are now going ⁠to continue pulling out all stops.”

Police in the province of Gauteng said on Sunday morning they had launched a manhunt for the unidentified eight suspects in the Johannesburg tavern shooting, with no arrests yet made.

“It is alleged that patrons were drinking inside and outside the tavern when the suspects arrived and opened fire on those outside,” a police spokesperson, Capt Tintswalo Sibeko, said in a statement.

“The suspects then entered the tavern and continued shooting at patrons inside. The suspects were reportedly armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols. They allegedly searched some patrons and took their cellphones before fleeing the scene in two unidentified motor vehicles. Two vehicles were also set alight during the incident.”

While many local residents did not want to speak about the shooting, one said that illegal goldminers were active in the area. Gauteng province’s police commissioner, Tommy Mthombeni, told reporters that one of their lines of inquiry was that the shooting was part of a “turf war in terms of illegal mining”.

Illegal miners, known as zama zamas, which means “to take a chance” in Zulu, are usually part of powerful gangs, with multiple mass shooting incidents around Johannesburg blamed on them in recent years.

Mthombeni also said Saturday’s shooting could have been retaliation for another at the same tavern about a month ago.

Western Cape police said they had set up a team led by serious violent crime detectives to investigate the Cape Town shooting, in which the gunmen entered the shinsanyama venue at about 1.46am on Sunday and starting shooting at customers.

“Five individuals died on the scene while five others succumbed to injuries sustained after being transported to medical facilities,” the statement said. “Eleven others are receiving medical treatment for injuries sustained … Detectives are hard at work in search of the perpetrators of the shooting incident, with no arrests effected yet. The identities of the deceased persons will be released once their next of kin are informed.”

A police official said that “business jealousy might have been the issue”, citing reports that people had been buying cheaper alcohol elsewhere and then bringing it to the venue to drink.

South Africans are already reeling after the discovery of numerous women’s bodies near Johannesburg’s airport since July, most of which were found in the last few weeks. The killings led to renewed anger about high rates of gender-based violence in the country, and have piled pressure on police and politicians to do more about it.

Alongside this, the Madlanga commission judicial inquiry has been examining allegations of corruption and criminality within the police in televised hearings for the past year.

South Africa had a murder rate of almost 40 per 100,000 people in 2024, according to the UN office on drugs and crime. That was the ninth-highest in the world that year, with only Caribbean countries higher.

In the 12 months to 30 June, more than 22,700 people were murdered in South Africa, according to police data.

Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report

world.title: ‘It’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces’: Cape Town divided over plan to remove its monkeys
world.snippet: Two troops of chacma baboons are breaking into homes and shops but animal rights activists insist coexistence is the answer Cape Town’s c...
world.content:
Cape Town’s city council has said it will “imminently” round up two baboon troops coming into repeated conflict with residents. The animals will be sterilised and permanently moved to a newly constructed sanctuary. The plan has been fiercely criticised by animal rights activists, who say the monkeys should remain roaming freely, and that less destructive options have not been properly considered.

Cape Town’s baboon problem has been brewing since the 2000s, after the city stopped culling troops in the late 1990s after pressure from the public. But in the past two years it has reached boiling point. A 2025 census found that the population had grown by a third since 2000, from 360 baboons to 493, now living in 12 managed troops.

As a result of the population boom, troops of chacma baboons on the city’s peninsula regularly rip off roof sheeting, sneak into unlocked cars and raid food pantries. Some monkeys are now staying up late into the night to break into homes in Simon’s Town and nab snacks from convenience stores. Residents can no longer barbecue or host garden parties for fear of the marauding baboons.

“It’s depreciated property values because it’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces and paw prints, and you know they’re coming every day,” said Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town who has long studied the local baboons.

Cape Town’s geography is partially to blame. Much of the problem is confined to the Cape Peninsula, a narrow sliver of land stretching from the city centre to Cape Point. Here, baboons are boxed in between the steep, protected area of Table Mountain national park and the sprawling urban development that stretches to the Atlantic Ocean.

“The underlying issue is that baboons will seek low-lying land. That is their natural drive – it’s better access to water and more productive vegetation,” said Joselyn Mormile, who leads the Cape Baboon Partnership (CBP), a nonprofit organisation that works with the city and local conservation authorities to manage the baboons. “But throughout the peninsula, we’ve developed most of those places. It’s a constant battle between the two.”

Initially, the CBP’s 2025 management plan proposed to move four troops to a sanctuary. That was revised, Mormile said, to give two other troops living in the northern section of the peninsula “the benefit of the doubt to see if they can adjust in that remaining space … We believe that they could settle quite nicely.”

The baboons have proved an especially divisive – and expensive – issue. Cape Town’s baboon management programme costs about 20m rand for 18 months (£920,000), with full-time rangers watching over most of the troops to try to head off any trouble.

In addition to moving the Waterfall and Seaforth troops to a sanctuary, a baboon-proof northern boundary fence will be erected between urban areas and nearby mountains.

Animal rights activists, who have been staging peaceful protests for months, and some scientists say the city should build a fence to exclude the Waterfall and Seaforth troops rather than remove the animals from their environment.

However, O’Riain said it was likely that the baboons would simply move along to the next area of low-lying land where the fence ends, as there was not enough food for the baboons behind the proposed southern fenced area.

Opponents argue that removing the other baboons will cause long-term psychological distress and social disruption, and that the baboons play an important ecological role by dispersing plant seeds.

Chacma baboons are not considered endangered. And the welfare of the animals is already in question: baboons are being poisoned, hit by cars, chased by dogs and shot.

“No one should ever shoot a baboon, but if people feel the authorities are not doing anything, they will take action – and that action is never nice,” O’Riain said. “Just a few days ago, a baboon was shot straight through the chest.

“How many more millions of rand are we going to throw into these troops only to end up in exactly the same place in another 10 years’ time?” he said. “Which is shocking baboon welfare, shocking baboon health, and a very poor quality of life for the people who are living in these areas.”

Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.
